qAndA.answer: Antibodies are depicted as "ninja warriors" holding ninja stars, symbolizing their role in fighting invaders.
qAndA.question: What visual metaphor is used to represent antibodies in the video?

qAndA.answer: Disulfide bridges connect the light and heavy chains of antibodies, shown visually with connecting lines.
qAndA.question: What type of bond connects the polypeptide chains in an antibody?

qAndA.answer: Antibodies can "tag" antigens, making them more susceptible to immune system attacks.
qAndA.question: Besides neutralizing antigens, what other function do antibodies perform?

qAndA.answer: Monoclonal antibodies are antibodies cloned in laboratory settings.
qAndA.question: What is the term used to describe antibodies that are produced in a laboratory?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: If this is the first time we've heard about antibodies, you may not know how important they are.
Antibodies are one of the warriors inside our body helping us fight of nasty invading
particles.
They are a type of protein and a key component of our immune system.
If a person doesn't produce or overproduces antibodies in the body, the person will become
very ill.
Another way to antibodies come from.
Antibodies circulate in the bloodstream and can appear anywhere throughout the body.
The function is to recognize bad agents called antigens and then trigger further chemical
reactions in the body to remove the antigens.
Antigens are foreign substances that are capable of triggering an immune response.
They can be viruses, fungi, bacteria and some non-living substances such as toxins,
chemicals and foreign particles.
They can even be allergens like dust, pollen or certain foods that cause allergic reactions.
Antibodies are produced in the immune system in response to the presence of an antigen.
So what do antibodies look like?
Antibodies are also known as immunoglobulin.
They are generally a wide-shaped protein consisting of four polypeptides, two identical light
chains and two identical heavy chains.
The terms light and heavy simply mean larger and smaller.
The four polypeptine chains are connected by disulfide bridges.
Here, at the top of each arm are the antigen binding sites.
These are really important parts for attacking and invading antigens.
Similar to the locking key mechanism in enzymes, the shape of the antigen binding site is specific
to the antigen it's targeting.
If part of the antigen fits into the antigen binding site, the antivari recognizes the foreign
antigen and bind it in.
This stops the antigen from causing more damage elsewhere.
Two identical binding site means any given antivari can bind simultaneously to two identical
antigens.
Millions of antivari will slightly different top structures exist, with each variant
binding to a different antigen.
This enormous diversity of antivari allows the immune system to recognize and equally
diverse range of antigens.
By binding in an antigen, an antivari can stop the antigen from entering or damaging
cells.
This is known as mutualizing.
The antivari can also take the antigen for attack by other parts of the immune system.
In mammals, they are five immunoglobulin isotopes.
